summary: Defines a Port Control Protocol (PCP) option that lets a client learn the IPv6 prefixes used by a PCP-controlled NAT64 device to build IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses. This is needed for communication to work when IPv4 addresses are passed around in referrals.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator turns old-style addresses into new-style ones by adding a special beginning. This lets a device ask the translator what that special beginning is.

questions: how to discover nat64 prefix with pcp
how to discover the nat64 prefix with pcp
what is the pcp prefix64 option
subtitle: A PCP option that tells an IPv6-only host which prefix its NAT64 uses to turn IPv4 addresses into IPv6 ones.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only host behind a NAT64 cannot use an IPv4 address it receives in a referral, and it cannot build the matching IPv6 address without knowing the NAT64 prefix.
tldr.mechanism: The PREFIX64 option (code 129) lets a PCP client ask the PCP server controlling the NAT64 for its Pref64::/n and suffix, optionally tied to lists of IPv4 destination prefixes.
tldr.outcome: The host can synthesize IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses itself, including for applications that do not use DNS, and can use DNSSEC in the presence of NAT64.

today: RFC 7225 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and Use Cases
sections.content:
A NAT64 builds IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses from a prefix called Pref64::/n (RFC 6146 and RFC 6052). RFC 7225 defines a new Port Control Protocol (PCP) option so a client can learn that prefix and suffix from a PCP-controlled NAT64.

The listed goals are to learn the prefix, avoid stale prefixes, discover multiple prefixes, use DNSSEC with NAT64, discover non-null suffixes, support destination-based prefixes, and associate a prefix with a specific NAT64. The RFC says this solves all the issues identified in RFC 7051, unlike RFC 7050.

Two use cases are given. A host with DNS64 in its stub resolver can synthesize AAAA records itself, and because synthetic records cannot be validated in a host, knowing the prefix allows DNSSEC. In application referrals, an entity passes an IPv4 address to a peer. Examples are SIP/SDP, WebRTC and BitTorrent, where an IPv6-only client cannot use the IPv4 address as given.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only speak new-style addresses and a friend hands you an old-style one, you cannot use it until you know the translator's special beginning. This option lets you ask for it.

sections.title: The PREFIX64 Option Format
sections.content:
The option uses Option Code 129 and follows the PCP option guidelines. It may appear in requests and responses, for the MAP and ANNOUNCE opcodes, at most once in a request and as many times as fit in the maximum PCP message size in a response.

  • Prefix64 Length: length of Pref64::/n in octets; allowed values are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 12.
  • Prefix64: the IPv6 prefix, either the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 or a Network-Specific Prefix. Address synthesis MUST follow RFC 6052.
  • Suffix: (12 minus Prefix64 Length) octets; absent for a /96 prefix.
  • IPv4 Prefix List: optional. An IPv4 Prefix Count (0 in a request, the number of subnets in a response) followed by IPv4 prefixes, each as a length and a 32-bit address. It maps IPv4 destination ranges to different Pref64::/n values.

If no list is returned, the client assumes the prefix is valid for any IPv4 destination. A wildcard 0.0.0.0/0 may be returned instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The message holds the translator's special beginning, how long it is, and optionally a list saying which old-style addresses use which beginning.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
A PCP server controlling a NAT64 SHOULD be configured to return the Pref64::/n and suffix. If no suffix is configured, the null suffix is the default. If the server honors the option but no Pref64::/n is configured, it MUST NOT include any PREFIX64 option.

A server MAY include the option in all MAP responses even if not requested, and MAY include it in ANNOUNCE messages. It MAY return several options in one message. Without IPv4 prefix lists, the first option carries the prefix to use for local synthesis and the others carry prefixes that let a host recognize synthesized addresses and avoid the NAT64. With lists, each option pairs a Pref64::/n with its IPv4 prefix list, and remaining prefixes follow.

If a distinct Pref64::/n or suffix is configured on the NAT64, the server SHOULD send an unsolicited ANNOUNCE to tell clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator's helper hands out its special beginning when asked, and sends a fresh note if the beginning ever changes.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A client includes the option in a MAP or ANNOUNCE request, with Prefix64 set to ::/96. It MUST be ready to receive several prefixes and MUST associate each prefix and suffix with the server it came from.

If the client fails to contact a server, for instance after moving to a new network, it SHOULD clear what it learned from that server, because stale prefixes are likely to fail. An invalid IPv4 prefix is ignored. New values replace old ones from the same server, including those in an unsolicited ANNOUNCE.

Without IPv4 prefix lists, the host uses the first option's prefix and suffix for synthesis, and can use the others to avoid the NAT64. With lists, the client MUST tie each IPv4 prefix to the Pref64::/n in the same option, and the host MUST choose the prefix by destination. How the values reach the operating system is implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks, remembers the answer for each helper, throws away old answers if the helper goes quiet, and picks the right beginning for each destination.

sections.title: Flow Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three non-normative examples. In the first, an IPv6-only client sends a MAP request with PREFIX64 and gets back 2001:db8:122:300::/56, then builds an IPv6 address for an IPv4-only server and opens a TCP connection through the NAT64.

In the second, an IPv6-only SIP user agent sends a MAP request carrying both PORT_SET and PREFIX64. It gets an external IPv4 address, a pair of ports and the prefix 2001:db8:122::/48. It builds an SDP offer with only IPv4 addresses and uses the prefix to convert the IPv4 address in the answer, so RTP and RTCP flow without an ALG at the NAT64.

In the third, a NAT64 maps 192.0.2.0/24 to 2001:db8:122:300::/56 and 198.51.100.0/24 to 2001:db8:122::/48. For the server 198.51.100.1 the client picks the second prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks for the beginning, then glues it in front of the old-style address to write the new-style one. If there are two translators' beginnings, it picks the one meant for that destination.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an attacker can change the Pref64::/n a host uses, the host's traffic goes to the altered prefix. The result can be a denial-of-service, flooding or man-in-the-middle attack. This could be done by altering messages from a real PCP server or by running a fake one.

Defenses against packet modification and spoofed server messages SHOULD be enabled; in some deployments, ACLs can allow only a trusted PCP server to talk to the client. PCP server discovery is out of scope.

The RFC adds that NAT64 with DNSSEC and PCP is better than no DNSSEC, but less safe than DNSSEC without DNS64, NAT64 and PCP. The best mitigation is IPv6 support in all endpoints, which reduces the need for synthesis.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster fakes the translator's answer, your messages could go to the wrong place, so only trust the real helper.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA allocated Option Code 129 for PREFIX64 in the optional-to-process range of the PCP option registry. That means a PCP server that does not understand the option can still process the rest of the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The option got its own number in the official list, 129.
